title: Iteration
summary: Do the same thing many times without copying code: apply functions to many columns with across(), keep rows by many columns at once, read twelve files into one table with map(), and write a file for each neighbourhood with walk2().

steps.title: Setup: library(tidyverse)

runs.purpose: load the tidyverse, which includes purrr

steps.explain: dplyr's `across()` repeats work over columns, and purrr's `map()` and `walk()` repeat it over anything else: files, sheets, groups.

steps.title: Many columns at once: across()

alternatives: weather = read_csv('data/weather.csv', show_col_types = FALSE) |> mutate(temp_c = na_if(temp_c, -99), wind_kmh = na_if(wind_kmh, -99))
runs.purpose: read the weather, replacing the sensor's -99 with NA in two columns at once, as `weather`
runs.task: Read `data/weather.csv`, then in `mutate()` replace -99 with `NA` in both `temp_c` and `wind_kmh` with `across()` and `\(x) na_if(x, -99)`. Store the result in `weather`.

alternatives: weather |> summarize(across(c(temp_c, rain_mm, wind_kmh), \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)))
runs.purpose: find the mean of every numeric column
runs.task: Find the mean of every numeric column of `weather`, leaving out missing values, with `across(where(is.numeric), …)` in `summarize()`.

steps.explain: `across()` applies a function to each of several columns. Its first argument picks the columns, by name as in `c(temp_c, wind_kmh)` or by a test such as `where(is.numeric)`; its second is the function, here written `\(x) …`, a short way of writing `function(x) …`. Lesson 18 fixed the -99 readings one column at a time; with `across()`, one line fixes both, and would fix ten. The year's mean temperature was {mean_temp} °C.

steps.title: Several functions, and their names

runs.code:
weather |>
  summarize(across(
    c(temp_c, wind_kmh),
    list(low = \(x) min(x, na.rm = TRUE), high = \(x) max(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
    .names = "{.col}_{.fn}"
  ))
alternatives: weather |> summarize(across(c(temp_c, wind_kmh), list(low = \(x) min(x, na.rm = TRUE), high = \(x) max(x, na.rm = TRUE))))
runs.purpose: find the lowest and highest temperature and wind speed, naming each result
runs.task: Find the lowest and highest `temp_c` and `wind_kmh`: give `across()` a named list of two functions, `low` and `high`, and name the results with `.names = "{.col}_{.fn}"`.

steps.explain: Given a named list of functions, `across()` applies each one to each column: two columns and two functions make four results. `.names` says how to name them, `{.col}` standing for the column's name and `{.fn}` for the function's, so the columns read `temp_c_low`, `temp_c_high` and so on. Without `.names`, `across()` names them the same way.

steps.title: Rows by many columns: if_any()

runs.purpose: keep the hours with any reading missing
runs.task: Keep the rows of `weather` where any of `temp_c`, `rain_mm` and `wind_kmh` is missing, with `if_any()` and `is.na`.

steps.explain: `filter()` needs one `TRUE` or `FALSE` per row, while a test applied across columns gives one per column. `if_any()` combines them with or: a row is kept if the test holds in any of the columns. `if_all()` combines them with and. {n_any_na} hours have a reading missing, all of them from the -99 codes; the sensor gaps have no rows at all.

steps.title: Many files: map() and list_rbind()

runs.purpose: list the monthly export files, as `paths`
runs.task: List the `.csv` files in `data/exports` with `fs::dir_ls()` and `glob = "*.csv"`, and store them in `paths`.

alternatives: exports = paths |> map(function(path) read_csv(path, skip = 1, na = c('', 'n/a', '-'), show_col_types = FALSE)) |> list_rbind(names_to = 'file')
runs.purpose: read each file the same way and stack them, with a column naming the file each row came from, as `exports`
runs.task: Read every file in `paths` with `map()` and `\(path) read_csv(path, skip = 1, na = c("", "n/a", "-"), show_col_types = FALSE)`, then stack the results with `list_rbind(names_to = "file")`. Store the result in `exports`.

steps.explain: `map()` calls a function once for each element of a vector and returns a list of the results: here, {n_paths} tibbles, one per month. `list_rbind()` stacks them into one, {n_exports} rows, and `names_to` keeps each element's name, the file's path, in a column. `show_col_types = FALSE` stops `read_csv()` reporting the columns of all twelve files. Lesson 7 read these files with one `read_csv()` call, which takes many files itself; `map()` works for any function that reads one thing at a time, such as `read_excel()` in lesson 20.

steps.title: Many outputs: walk2()

runs.code:
by_area <- read_csv("data/stations.csv") |>
  nest(.by = neighbourhood) |>
  mutate(path = str_c("neighbourhoods/", neighbourhood, ".csv"))
alternatives: by_area = read_csv('data/stations.csv', show_col_types = FALSE) |> nest(.by = neighbourhood) |> mutate(path = paste0('neighbourhoods/', neighbourhood, '.csv'))
runs.purpose: split the stations into one table per neighbourhood, each with a file name, as `by_area`
runs.task: Read `data/stations.csv`, nest it by `neighbourhood` with `nest(.by = neighbourhood)`, and add `path`, "neighbourhoods/" + the neighbourhood + ".csv", with `str_c()`. Store the result in `by_area`.

runs.purpose: make the folder the files go in
write each neighbourhood's stations to its own CSV file
runs.task: Write each table in `by_area$data` to its file in `by_area$path`, with `walk2()` and `write_csv`.

steps.explain: `nest()` puts each neighbourhood's stations in a list-column, `data`, one table per row. `walk2()` walks along two vectors side by side, the tables and their paths, calling `write_csv()` with each pair. A `walk` function is a `map` for functions you call for what they do, here writing a file, rather than for what they return. The Files pane shows {n_areas} files in `neighbourhoods`.
